note — the bold part is what the card te: Counting, one is eins; before a noun it becomes the article ein.
zwei. On the phone Germans often say zwo, so it is not mixed up with drei.
For age, sein and the number are enough: ist drei.
Euro takes no plural ending after a number: zwei Euro.
vier: the ie is a long i, as in English see.
fünf, with ü.
sechs: the chs sounds like ks.
sieben has two syllables: sie-ben.
acht, with the ch from the back of the throat.
neun: eu sounds like oy in boy.
zehn: the z sounds like ts, the h is silent.
elf is a word of its own, like English eleven.

English: How old is the dog? – He is **twelve**.
German: Wie alt ist der Hund? – Er ist **zwölf**.
note — the bold part is what the card te: zwölf, like elf, is not built from zehn.
From 13, the unit comes first, then zehn: drei-zehn, like thir-teen.
vier + zehn, written as one word.
fünf + zehn: fünfzehn.
sechzehn drops the s of sechs: not sechszehn.
siebzehn drops the -en of sieben: not siebenzehn.
acht + zehn, nothing dropped.

English: How old are you? (one friend) – I am **nineteen**.
German: Wie alt bist du? – Ich bin **neunzehn**.
note — the bold part is what the card te: neun + zehn: neunzehn.
zwanzig: the tens end in -zig, and zwei shortens to zwan-.
zwanzig Euro: Euro stays the same after any number.
null before a noun is a casual way of saying none at all, as with English zero.
null: zero. Counting starts with null, eins.

English: Is the cat ten? – No, she is **eleven**.
German: Ist die Katze zehn? – Nein, sie ist **elf**.
note — the bold part is what the card te: A question with the verb first gets ja or nein; elf is eleven.
sieben, acht: seven, eight.

English: What does the bread cost? – **Three** euros.
note — the bold part is what the card te: drei Euro: the number, then Euro without a plural ending.

English: Does the coffee cost **two** or three euros?
German: Kostet der Kaffee **zwei** oder drei Euro?
note — the bold part is what the card te: A yes/no question with the verb first; zwei Euro.
Before a noun one is the article ein, and kostet takes the accusative: einen Euro.
der Euro, so einen Euro, whatever the thing that costs it.
Ages work the same for everyone: sein + the number.

English: Why does the tea cost **twenty** euros?
note — the bold part is what the card te: Question word first, then kostet, then the subject.
